propositions.text: The applicant applied for judicial review of a decision by the Refugee Appeal Division dated May 24, 2023.
propositions.quote: The applicant applied for judicial review of a decision by the Refugee Appeal Division (the “RAD”) dated May 24, 2023.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant applied for judicial review of the RAD's May 24, 2023 decision, says the court.

propositions.text: The RAD dismissed the applicant's appeal from the RPD, both concluding he is excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E and section 98 IRPA.
propositions.quote: The RAD dismissed the applicant’s appeal from the Refugee Protection Division (the “RPD”). Both concluded that the applicant is not a Convention Refugee and not a person in need of protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (the “IRPA") because he is excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E of the Refugee Convention and section 98 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD and RPD both found the applicant excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E and section 98 IRPA, says the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: The applicant contends the RAD's decision was unreasonable and should be set aside, applying Vavilov principles.
propositions.quote: The applicant contended that the RAD’s decision was unreasonable and should be set aside, applying the principles in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, [2019] 4 SCR 563.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the RAD's decision was unreasonable and should be set aside, citing Vavilov, says the applicant.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed for the reasons below.
propositions.quote: For the reasons below, the application is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review, says the court.

propositions.text: The applicant is a Pakistani citizen claiming IRPA protection due to fear of Tehrik-e-Taliban threats from his advocacy work.
propositions.quote: The applicant is a citizen of Pakistan. His claim for IRPA protection was based on a fear of the Tehrik-e-Taliban in Pakistan because of threats against him arising from his work advocating for religious minorities and promoting COVID-19 vaccines in his community.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant is a Pakistani citizen fearing Tehrik-e-Taliban threats due to advocacy work, says the court.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the applicant's claim, finding exclusion from refugee protection due to his status in Italy under Zeng test.
propositions.quote: By decision dated January 30, 2023, the RPD rejected the applicant’s claim because it concluded that the applicant was excluded from refugee protection because of his status in Italy. The RPD applied the test set out in Zeng v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FCA 118, [2011] 4 FCR 3, at para 28.

propositions.text: Applicant did not have current Italian status substantially similar to nationals but had previously and lost it voluntarily by coming to Canada.
propositions.quote: While the applicant did not have status in Italy that was substantially similar to an Italian national at the time of the hearing, the RPD concluded that he previously had that status and lost it voluntarily by coming to Canada.

propositions.text: Applicant still had avenues to regain Italian status; RPD found his behaviour consistent with asylum shopping.
propositions.quote: According to the RPD’s decision, the applicant still had avenues to regain that status and his behaviour was consistent with “asylum shopping”.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the applicant excluded due to prior Italian status lost voluntarily and asylum shopping, applying Zeng test, says the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Applicant argued to RAD he did not have permanent status in Italy, correcting prior mistaken testimony based on counsel's erroneous advice.
propositions.quote: On appeal to the RAD, the applicant argued that he did not have permanent status in Italy. Although he testified before the RPD that he had permanent status, he filed an affidavit on the appeal in which he advised that his testimony was mistaken and based on (allegedly erroneous) advice given to him by his former counsel in the RPD proceedings.

propositions.text: Applicant argued to RAD that he had only temporary status in Italy based on country evidence and Italian status cards.
propositions.quote: Based on country evidence and evidence related to status cards issued to him by the Italian government, the applicant argued to the RAD that he had only temporary status in Italy and was therefore not excluded by Article 1E.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argued to RAD he had only temporary Italian status, correcting prior mistaken testimony, says the applicant.

propositions.text: RAD disagreed with applicant's claim that RPD erred in finding he had an Italian permanent resident card.
propositions.quote: The RAD did not agree with the applicant’s position that the RPD erred by finding that he had an Italian permanent resident card.

propositions.text: RAD considered applicant's testimony and Italian card evidence and upheld RPD's exclusion under Article 1E.
propositions.quote: The RAD considered both the applicant’s testimony and the evidence related to the applicant’s Italian cards. The RAD concluded that the RPD was correct to find that the applicant was excluded under Article 1E.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD considered evidence and upheld RPD's finding that applicant was excluded under Article 1E, says the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: The applicant now challenges the RAD's decision.
propositions.quote: The applicant now challenges the RAD’s decision.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant challenges the RAD's decision, says the court.

propositions.text: The standard of review of the RAD's substantive decision is reasonableness per Vavilov; onus on applicant to show unreasonableness.
propositions.quote: The standard of review of the RAD’s substantive decision is reasonableness, as described in Vavilov. The onus is on the applicant to demonstrate that the decision is unreasonable: Vavilov, at paras 75 and 100.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is reasonableness under Vavilov, with onus on applicant to prove unreasonableness.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review is deferential, evaluating if decision is transparent, intelligible, justified, based on coherent analysis and facts and law.
propositions.quote: Reasonableness review is a deferential and disciplined evaluation of whether an administrative decision is transparent, intelligible and justified: Mason v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 SCC 21, at paras 8, 63; Vavilov, at paras 12-13 and 15. The starting point is the reasons provided by the decision maker, which are read holistically and contextually, and in conjunction with the record that was before the decision maker. A reasonable decision is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrained the decision maker: Mason, at paras 8, 59-61, 66; Vavilov, esp. at paras 85, 91-97, 103, 105-106 and 194.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains reasonableness review is deferential, assessing if decision is justified, transparent, and coherent, citing Mason and Vavilov.

propositions.text: Court cannot re-assess evidence or merits; intervention only if decision-maker misapprehended evidence, ignored critical evidence, or lacked rational support.
propositions.quote: It is not the role of the Court to re-assess or re-weigh the evidence, or to provide its own view of the merits. Thus, it is not permissible for the Court to come to its own view of the merits of the application and then measure the impugned decision against the Court’s own assessment: Mason, at para 62; Vavilov, at paras 83, 125; Delios v. Canada (Attorney General), 2015 FCA 117, at para 28. With respect to the factual constraints in the evidence, the Court may intervene only in limited circumstances, for example when the decision maker has fundamentally misapprehended the evidence before it, ignored critical evidence, made findings without any rational supporting evidence or failed to account for evidence before it that ran counter to its conclusion: Vavilov, at para 126; Federal Courts Act, paragraph 18.1(4)(d); Maritime Employers Association v. Syndicat des débardeurs (Canadian Union of Public Employees, Local 375), 2023 FCA 93, at paras 115-117; Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Galindo Camayo, 2022 FCA 50, at para 78.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it cannot re-weigh evidence or merits, intervening only for serious errors like ignoring critical evidence, citing authorities.

propositions.text: Court must find sufficiently serious shortcomings, more than minor missteps, to intervene and find decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: To intervene, the reviewing court must be satisfied that there are “sufficiently serious shortcomings” in the decision, such that it does not exhibit sufficient justification, intelligibility and transparency. Flaws or shortcomings must be more than a “minor misstep”; the problem must be sufficiently central or significant to the outcome to render the decision unreasonable: Vavilov, at para 100.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains intervention requires serious shortcomings central to outcome, not minor missteps, citing Vavilov.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD failed to perform independent analysis and misunderstood affidavit evidence, misapplied country info, misclassified Italian status cards, and failed to explain rejection of affidavit testimony.
propositions.quote: On this application for judicial review, the applicant raised the following arguments to challenge the reasonableness of the RAD’s decision: a)The RAD did not perform an independent analysis of the evidence, as it was required to do; and b)The RAD misunderstood or ignored the applicant’s affidavit evidence, improperly applied country information and misclassified the applicant’s Italian status card(s), and failed to provide an explanation for why it did not accept his testimony by affidavit on the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD failed independent analysis, misunderstood affidavit evidence, misapplied country info, misclassified Italian cards, and failed to explain affidavit rejection.

propositions.text: The RAD's decision was reasonable; no basis to set it aside applying Vavilov principles.
propositions.quote: I conclude that the RAD’s decision was reasonable. I find no basis for the Court to set aside the RAD’s decision on these grounds, applying the principles in Vavilov.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the RAD's decision was reasonable and finds no basis to set it aside under Vavilov.

propositions.text: Applicant argued RAD failed to conduct independent analysis and merely affirmed RPD reasoning.
propositions.quote: The applicant argued that the RAD did not carry out its proper role on appeal by conducting an independent analysis of the evidence, and instead, merely affirmed the reasoning of the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD failed independent analysis and just affirmed RPD reasoning.

propositions.text: RAD's 50-paragraph analysis shows it applied correct test, analyzed testimony and evidence, and fulfilled its role to decide if RPD was correct.
propositions.quote: This position is untenable, given the RAD’s 50-paragraph analysis. That analysis set out the correct test from Zeng (RAD’s reasons, paragraph 23), analyzed the applicant’s testimony about his status in Italy and the cards issued to him (paragraphs 25-38), assessed the applicant’s Italian cards and his arguments about the country evidence (paragraphs 28, 37, 39-42) and considered whether the RPD was correct in applying the balance of the Zeng test (paras 43-47). The RAD described its role as “to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision”. It adequately performed that role.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD performed independent analysis, applying correct test and assessing evidence, fulfilling its role.

propositions.text: Applicant's submissions re-argue merits; court cannot review evidence anew or provide own view on merits.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s written submissions effectively re-argued the merits of his position before the RAD, that on the basis of his affidavit filed on appeal and a correct understanding of the evidence related to his Italian status card, he had temporary (not permanent) status in Italy. As noted above, it is not the role of this Court to review the evidence anew and provide its own views on the merits of these issues: Vavilov, at paras 83, 125.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes applicant re-argues merits, but court cannot review evidence anew or provide own view on merits.

propositions.text: There was debate about applicant's Italian cards and status; applicant testified repeatedly he had permanent status card taken in 2021.
propositions.quote: There was considerable debate before the RPD and the RAD about what kinds of cards the applicant held at different times, what status the cards conveyed on him and what card was taken from the applicant on his re-entry to Italy in 2021. In a long passage of questions and answers quoted by the RAD, the applicant testified repeatedly before the RPD that he had a card that gave him permanent status in Italy. He referred to a card that Italian officials took from him when he returned to Italy in 2021.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds debate about applicant's Italian cards and status, with applicant testifying he had permanent status card taken in 2021.

propositions.text: RAD reviewed evidence, referred to country evidence, and determined nature of status cards and which was taken at border.
propositions.quote: The RAD reviewed the evidence and determined the nature of the status cards, and which card was taken from the applicant at the border. The RAD’s analysis referred to country evidence from the National Documentation Package for Italy.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted RAD misclassified status card and that properly classified he only held temporary status card consistent with affidavit testimony.
propositions.quote: The applicant submitted that the RAD erroneously misclassified the status card given to the applicant and that properly classified, he only held a card gave him temporary status (consistent with his testimony on appeal).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD reviewed evidence and country info to determine status cards; applicant argues RAD misclassified card and he held only temporary status.

propositions.text: The applicant has not persuaded me that it was not open to the RAD to reach its conclusions and overall decision.
propositions.quote: The applicant has not persuaded me that it was not open to the RAD to reach the conclusions and overall decision it did.

propositions.text: The applicant has not shown that the RAD fundamentally misapprehended the evidence about his status cards or country information.
propositions.quote: The applicant has not shown that the RAD fundamentally misapprehended the evidence about his status cards or the applicable country information.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant failed to show the RAD erred in its conclusions or misapprehended evidence about status cards or country information.

propositions.text: The RAD disregarded his affidavit evidence that he believed his residency card conveyed only temporary status in Italy and that he was mistaken in testifying he had permanent status.
propositions.quote: The applicant submitted that the RAD disregarded his affidavit evidence that he “always believed that [his] residency card only conveyed temporary status in Italy” and that he was mistaken when he testified at the RPD hearing and said that he had permanent status in Italy.

propositions.text: The RAD provided no explanation for ignoring his appeal evidence.
propositions.quote: The applicant argued that the RAD provided no explanation for why it ignored his appeal evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the RAD ignored his affidavit and gave no explanation for ignoring his appeal evidence.

propositions.text: I do not agree that the RAD disregarded the affidavit evidence or failed to explain its reasoning.
propositions.quote: I do not agree.

propositions.text: The RAD was aware of the affidavit and contents relied on by the applicant in this Court.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s reasons show that it was aware of the affidavit and the contents relied on by the applicant in this Court.

propositions.text: The RAD found the applicant’s evidence about permanent residence status came from himself and it was reasonable to expect consistency about his status.
propositions.quote: [33] I am not persuaded by the Appellant’s argument on appeal that he was granted temporary status only in the form of a Sussidiaria and the RPD Member erred by attributing a particular status (permanent residence) to him that he did not have as the evidence about him having permanent residence status came from the Appellant himself and it is reasonable to expect that he would know and be consistent about the status he obtained.

propositions.text: The RAD was not persuaded by the applicant’s claim that he believed his residency card conveyed only temporary status and that he testified about permanent status due to counsel’s advice.
propositions.quote: [34] The Appellant contends on appeal that he always believed his residency card (the card disclosed after the [RPD] hearing) only conveyed temporary status in Italy and that he only testified at the hearing about it being a permanent card because his former Counsel (who represented him at the hearing) had advised him that in Canada, it was considered to have conveyed permanent resident status. He also indicates that he had given this card to his former Counsel to disclose to the RPD and was unaware that it had not been submitted for the hearing. I am also not persuaded by this.

propositions.text: The RAD found it not credible that the applicant would testify as he did if he always understood his status to be temporary.
propositions.quote: [35] Had the Appellant always understood his status to be temporary, he ought to have said this and if the card that he had and/or his status never changed from that of “Sussidiaria” or subsidiary protection, it is not credible that he would have testified as he did; […]

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with the applicant, finding the RAD considered his affidavit and explained why it rejected his claim about temporary status.

propositions.text: The RAD did not expressly attribute passages to the applicant’s affidavit but used language tracking relevant aspects of it.
propositions.quote: While the RAD did not expressly attribute these passages to the applicant’s affidavit, the RAD used language that in part tracked the relevant aspects of the applicant’s affidavit on appeal

propositions.text: Much of the applicant’s affidavit on appeal was not evidence but described arguments from his counsel on information and belief.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, much of the applicant’s affidavit on appeal consisted of information that was not actually evidence, but instead described arguments to be made on the appeal sourced from his appeal counsel on information and belief.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD’s reasons tracked the applicant’s affidavit and that much of the affidavit was argument, not evidence.

propositions.text: The RAD’s reasons were responsive to the applicant’s position and adequately explained why it disagreed with his affidavit evidence.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s reasons were responsive to the applicant’s position and his affidavit evidence that he was mistaken during his RPD testimony, and adequately explained why the RAD member disagreed with his position.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD adequately responded to and explained its disagreement with the applicant’s affidavit evidence.

propositions.text: The applicant has not demonstrated that the RAD made a reviewable error under Vavilov principles.
propositions.quote: The applicant has not demonstrated that the RAD made a reviewable error under Vavilov principles.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: The application is therefore dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the applicant failed to show a reviewable error and dismisses the application.

propositions.text: Neither party proposed a question for certification and none arises.
propositions.quote: Neither party proposed a question for certification and none arises.

propositions.text: The application is dismissed and no question is certified under paragraph 74(d) of the IRPA.
propositions.quote: THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The application is dismissed. No question is certified under paragraph 74(d) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application and certifies no question under IRPA paragraph 74(d).
